\section{Introduction}

The \emph{flag variety} $\Fl_n$ parametrises complete flags
\[
\mathcal{F}: \quad \{0\} = V_0 \subset V_1 \subset \cdots \subset V_n = \mathbb{C}^n,
\qquad \dim V_k = k,
\]
and is one of the central objects of algebraic geometry and representation
theory. The Borel subgroup $B \subset GL_n(\mathbb{C})$ of upper-triangular
invertible matrices acts on $\Fl_n$ with finitely many orbits, the
\emph{Schubert cells}, indexed by the symmetric group $S_n$ (the Weyl group of
type $A_{n-1}$). The \emph{Bruhat decomposition} organises these cells, and the
\emph{Bruhat order} describes their closures:
\[
X_u \subseteq \overline{X_v} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u \le v
\ \text{ in the Bruhat order.}
\]

When one considers a \emph{product} of flag manifolds and the diagonal $B$
action, each orbit acquires a pair of Weyl-group parameters via the two
projections. The natural conjecture, which this paper certifies at the
order-theoretic level, is that the closure relation on orbits coincides with
the restriction of the \emph{product Bruhat order} to the image of the
parametrising map:
\[
\mathcal{O}_1 \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{O}_2}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\varphi(\mathcal{O}_1) \le \varphi(\mathcal{O}_2)
\ \text{ in } (S_n, \le) \times (S_n, \le).
\]

Our contribution is to isolate and prove the combinatorial skeleton on which
this statement rests. We make no geometric assumptions: we build the Bruhat
order from the Ehresmann rank criterion and prove that it is a partial order,
that it is invariant under inversion (so the two projections carry compatible
orders), that it has explicit extremes, and that the two-projection map
$w \mapsto (w, w^{-1})$ is an order embedding into the product order whose
image realises the closure relation.

\section{Definitions}

Throughout, $n$ is a positive integer and $S_n$ denotes the group of
permutations of $\{1, \dots, n\}$, with $\id$ the identity permutation.

\begin{definition}[Inversion set and length]
The \emph{inversion set} of $\sigma \in S_n$ is
\[
\Inv(\sigma) = \{\, (i, j) : i < j \ \text{and}\ \sigma(j) < \sigma(i) \,\},
\]
and the \emph{length} is $\ell(\sigma) = \#\Inv(\sigma)$, the number of
adjacent transpositions in a reduced word for $\sigma$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Rank count]
For $w \in S_n$ and indices $i, j$, the \emph{Ehresmann rank count} is
\[
\rk_w(i, j) = \#\{\, k \le i : w(k) \le j \,\}.
\]
The array $(\rk_w(i,j))_{i,j}$ is the \emph{rank matrix} of $w$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Bruhat order]
For $u, v \in S_n$,
\[
u \le v \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \rk_v(i, j) \le \rk_u(i, j)
\ \text{ for all } i, j.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Product Bruhat order]
On pairs in $S_n \times S_n$,
\[
(p_1, p_2) \le (q_1, q_2) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p_1 \le q_1 \ \text{and}\ p_2 \le q_2.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Two-projection map]
The map $\varphi : S_n \to S_n \times S_n$, $\varphi(w) = (w, w^{-1})$, is the
combinatorial shadow of the two projections of a product of flag manifolds.
\end{definition}

\section{Inversion invariance via the transpose identity}

\begin{theorem}[Transpose identity]
For every $w \in S_n$ and all $i, j$, $\ \rk_{w^{-1}}(i, j) = \rk_{w}(j, i)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Both sides count points of the permutation graph in a rectangular window. The
bijection $k \mapsto w^{-1}(k)$ sends $\{ k \le i : w^{-1}(k) \le j\}$ onto
$\{ m \le j : w(m) \le i \}$, since $k \le i$ and $w^{-1}(k) = m \le j$ is
equivalent to $m \le j$ and $w(m) = k \le i$. Cardinalities are preserved, and
the latter set has size $\rk_w(j, i)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Inversion invariance]
For all $u, v \in S_n$, $\ u \le v \iff u^{-1} \le v^{-1}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $u \le v$ then for all $i, j$, applying the transpose identity twice,
$\rk_{v^{-1}}(i,j) = \rk_v(j,i) \le \rk_u(j,i) = \rk_{u^{-1}}(i,j)$, so
$u^{-1} \le v^{-1}$. The converse follows since $(w^{-1})^{-1} = w$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
The two-projection map $\varphi(w) = (w, w^{-1})$ is an order embedding:
$u \le v \iff \varphi(u) \le \varphi(v)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\varphi(u) \le \varphi(v)$ means $u \le v$ and $u^{-1} \le v^{-1}$; by the
previous theorem each conjunct is equivalent to $u \le v$.
\end{proof}

\section{Antisymmetry: the rank matrix determines the permutation}

\begin{theorem}[Rank rigidity / antisymmetry]
If $u \le v$ and $v \le u$ then $u = v$. Equivalently, if
$\rk_u(i,j) = \rk_v(i,j)$ for all $i,j$, then $u = v$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Equality of the weak counts $\rk_u = \rk_v$ propagates to the strict counts
$c^{<}_w(i,j) = \#\{ k < i : w(k) \le j\}$ by shifting the row index down by
one (the boundary row $i=1$ has strict count $0$). The single-row difference
\[
\rk_w(i,j) - c^{<}_w(i,j) = \mathbf{1}[\, w(i) \le j \,]
\]
is a monotone $0/1$ step function of $j$ whose jump locates $w(i)$. Since these
indicators agree for $u$ and $v$ at every $j$, we get $u(i) = v(i)$ for all
$i$, hence $u = v$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Partial order]
The Bruhat order is reflexive, transitive, and antisymmetric, hence a partial
order on $S_n$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Reflexivity and transitivity follow directly from the defining inequalities on
rank counts; antisymmetry is the preceding theorem.
\end{proof}

\section{Extremes and the length characterisation}

\begin{theorem}[Bottom element]
$\id \le w$ for all $w \in S_n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\rk_{\id}(i,j) = \min(i,j)$ is the maximal possible rank count, so
$\rk_w(i,j) \le \rk_{\id}(i,j)$ for every $w$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Top element]
The reversal $w_0 : k \mapsto n+1-k$ satisfies $w \le w_0$ for all $w \in S_n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\rk_{w_0}(i,j) = \max(0,\, i+j-n)$ is the minimal rank count forced by the
marginals, so $\rk_{w_0}(i,j) \le \rk_w(i,j)$ for every $w$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Minimum $=$ length zero]
$w = \id$ if and only if $\ell(w) = 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\ell(w) = 0$ means $w$ has no inversions, hence is increasing, hence the
identity; and $\ell(\id) = 0$. Combined with the bottom-element theorem, the
unique inversion-free permutation is exactly the minimum.
\end{proof}

\section{The product order and the headline correspondence}

\begin{proposition}[Product order structure]
The product Bruhat order on $S_n \times S_n$ is a partial order with minimum
$(\id, \id)$ and maximum $(w_0, w_0)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Reflexivity, transitivity, and antisymmetry hold coordinatewise; the extremes
are the pairs of extremes.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Closure $=$ product Bruhat order]
For $\varphi(w) = (w, w^{-1})$,
\[
u \le v \iff \varphi(u) \le \varphi(v) \iff (u, u^{-1}) \le (v, v^{-1})
\ \text{ componentwise.}
\]
Hence the Bruhat relation on orbit parameters coincides with the restriction
of the product Bruhat order to the image of $\varphi$---the order-theoretic
statement of ``Bruhat order preserves closure relations for orbit strata.''
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\varphi(u) \le \varphi(v)$ unpacks to $u \le v$ and $u^{-1} \le v^{-1}$; by
inversion invariance the second conjunct is equivalent to the first, so the
componentwise comparison on the image reduces to the single comparison
$u \le v$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Under the parametrisation of orbit strata by pairs of Weyl-group elements,
$\mathcal{O}_1 \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{O}_2}$ if and only if the labels
compare componentwise in the product Bruhat order. The theorem certifies the
combinatorial half of this equivalence, turning a continuous closure question
into a finite rank-count comparison.
\end{remark}

\section{Algorithms}

\textbf{Rank matrix.} Given $w$, compute all $\rk_w(i,j)$ in $O(n^2)$ by prefix
sums over positions and values.

\textbf{Bruhat comparison.} To test $u \le v$, compare both rank matrices
entrywise in $O(n^2)$.

\textbf{Closure test on pairs.} To test $(u_1,v_1) \le (u_2,v_2)$, run the
comparison in each coordinate; for image pairs $(w, w^{-1})$ a single
comparison suffices by the correspondence theorem. By rank rigidity, the rank
matrix decodes back to $w$ by locating each row's $0\to 1$ jump.

\section{Applications}

Closure relations of Schubert cells control incidences and singularities of
Schubert varieties and the combinatorics of their cohomology; a rank-count
decision procedure makes them computable in quadratic time. $B$-orbits on
products of flag manifolds arise in representation theory, where the product
Bruhat order organises the strata. The rank matrix connects orbit closures to
domination of $0/1$-matrices, and the length statistic ties covering relations
to inversion counts and sorting.

\section{Discussion and future work}

We proposed: (1) an additive grading of the closure order by the sum of the
two Coxeter lengths; (2) strict length monotonicity, with covers raising
length by exactly one; (3) self-duality via the order-reversing involution
$w \mapsto w_0 w$; and (4) rigidity of the whole closure lattice under
entrywise rank-matrix domination.

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations
from typing import List, Tuple

Perm = Tuple[int, ...]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core combinatorial primitives
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def all_perms(n: int) -> List[Perm]:
    """All permutations of {0, ..., n-1}."""
    return list(permutations(range(n)))


def inverse(w: Perm) -> Perm:
    """Group inverse of a permutation: inv[w[k]] = k."""
    inv = [0] * len(w)
    for k, wk in enumerate(w):
        inv[wk] = k
    return tuple(inv)


def rk(w: Perm, i: int, j: int) -> int:
    """Ehresmann rank count: #{ k <= i : w[k] <= j }  (0-indexed)."""
    return sum(1 for k in range(i + 1) if w[k] <= j)


def rank_matrix(w: Perm) -> List[List[int]]:
    """The full n x n rank matrix of w."""
    n = len(w)
    return [[rk(w, i, j) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]

the closure of O2 if and only if the parametrising pairs satisfy the componentwise Bruhat

relation u <*> v increases the length by exactly one.

sending one extreme to the other is the natural next structural symmetry to certify.

    "demo": """"
Numerical demonstrations for:

    The Product Bruhat Order and the Closure of Orbit Strata
    on Products of Flag Manifolds

Everything is elementary and self-contained. A "permutation" is a tuple
`w` of length n that is a rearrangement of range(n); `w[k]` is the image of
position k (0-indexed throughout).

We verify, by direct computation on small symmetric groups, the results of
the paper:

  * the Ehresmann rank count  rk_w(i, j) = #{ k <= i : w[k] <= j }
  * the Bruhat order  u <= v  iff  rk_v(i,j) <= rk_u(i,j) for all i, j
  * the transpose identity   rk_{w^{-1}}(i, j) = rk_w(j, i)
  * inversion invariance     u <= v  iff  u^{-1} <= v^{-1}
  * antisymmetry             (u <= v and v <= u) => u == v
  * extremes                 id is minimum, reversal w0 is maximum
  * length zero              w == id  iff  #inversions(w) == 0
  * headline correspondence  u <= v  iff  (u,u^{-1}) <= (v,v^{-1})
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations
from typing import List, Tuple

Perm = Tuple[int, ...]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core combinatorial primitives
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def all_perms(n: int) -> List[Perm]:
    """All permutations of {0, ..., n-1}."""
    return list(permutations(range(n)))


def inverse(w: Perm) -> Perm:
    """Group inverse of a permutation: inv[w[k]] = k."""
    inv = [0] * len(w)
    for k, wk in enumerate(w):
        inv[wk] = k
    return tuple(inv)


def rk(w: Perm, i: int, j: int) -> int:
    """Ehresmann rank count: #{ k <= i : w[k] <= j }  (0-indexed)."""
    return sum(1 for k in range(i + 1) if w[k] <= j)


def rank_matrix(w: Perm) -> List[List[int]]:
    """The full n x n rank matrix of w."""
    n = len(w)
    return [[rk(w, i, j) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def bruhat_le(u: Perm, v: Perm) -> bool:
    """Bruhat order via the Ehresmann rank criterion: u <= v."""
    n = len(u)
    return all(rk(v, i, j) <= rk(u, i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(n))


def num_inversions(w: Perm) -> int:
    """Coxeter length: number of pairs i < j with w[i] > w[j]."""
    n = len(w)
    return sum(1 for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n) if w[i] > w[j])


def identity(n: int) -> Perm:
    return tuple(range(n))


def reversal(n: int) -> Perm:
    """The longest element w0: k |-> n-1-k."""
    return tuple(n - 1 - k for k in range(n))


def prod_bruhat_le(p: Tuple[Perm, Perm], q: Tuple[Perm, Perm]) -> bool:
    """Componentwise (product) Bruhat order."""
    return bruhat_le(p[0], q[0]) and bruhat_le(p[1], q[1])


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Verifications
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def check_transpose_identity(n: int) -> bool:
    """rk_{w^{-1}}(i, j) == rk_w(j, i) for all w, i, j."""
    for w in all_perms(n):
        wi = inverse(w)
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(n):
                if rk(wi, i, j) != rk(w, j, i):
                    return False
    return True


def check_inversion_invariance(n: int) -> bool:
    """u <= v  iff  u^{-1} <= v^{-1}."""
    perms = all_perms(n)
    for u in perms:
        for v in perms:
            if bruhat_le(u, v) != bruhat_le(inverse(u), inverse(v)):
                return False
    return True


def check_antisymmetry(n: int) -> bool:
    """(u <= v and v <= u) => u == v."""
    perms = all_perms(n)
    for u in perms:
        for v in perms:
            if bruhat_le(u, v) and bruhat_le(v, u) and u != v:
                return False
    return True


def check_extremes(n: int) -> bool:
    """id is the minimum and reversal is the maximum."""
    e, w0 = identity(n), reversal(n)
    return all(bruhat_le(e, w) and bruhat_le(w, w0) for w in all_perms(n))


def check_length_zero(n: int) -> bool:
    """w == id  iff  num_inversions(w) == 0."""
    e = identity(n)
    for w in all_perms(n):
        if (num_inversions(w) == 0) != (w == e):
            return False
    return True


def check_headline(n: int) -> bool:
    """u <= v  iff  (u, u^{-1}) <= (v, v^{-1}) componentwise."""
    perms = all_perms(n)
    for u in perms:
        for v in perms:
            lhs = bruhat_le(u, v)
            rhs = prod_bruhat_le((u, inverse(u)), (v, inverse(v)))
            if lhs != rhs:
                return False
    return True


def main() -> None:
    print("=" * 66)
    print("Bruhat order & closure of orbit strata -- numerical checks")
    print("=" * 66)

    # A concrete rank-matrix example.
    w: Perm = (2, 0, 3, 1)
    print(f"\nExample permutation w = {w}  (0-indexed)")
    print(f"  inverse(w)      = {inverse(w)}")
    print(f"  #inversions(w)  = {num_inversions(w)}")
    print("  rank matrix rk_w(i,j):")
    for row in rank_matrix(w):
        print("    ", row)

    # Transpose identity illustrated on the same w.
    print("\nTranspose identity  rk_{w^-1}(i,j) == rk_w(j,i):")
    n = len(w)
    ok = all(rk(inverse(w), i, j) == rk(w, j, i)
             for i in range(n) for j in range(n))
    print(f"  holds for w = {w}: {ok}")

    # A comparable and an incomparable pair in S_3.
    print("\nSample comparisons in S_3 (0-indexed):")
    for u, v in [((0, 1, 2), (2, 1, 0)),
                 ((1, 0, 2), (2, 0, 1)),
                 ((1, 0, 2), (0, 2, 1))]:
        print(f"  {u} <= {v} ?  {bruhat_le(u, v)}")

    # Exhaustive checks across small n.
    print("\nExhaustive verification of all theorems:")
    header = ("n", "transpose", "inv-inv", "antisym",
              "extremes", "len-zero", "headline")
    print("  " + "  ".join(f"{h:>10}" for h in header))
    for n in range(1, 6):
        results = (
            check_transpose_identity(n),
            check_inversion_invariance(n),
            check_antisymmetry(n),
            check_extremes(n),
            check_length_zero(n),
            check_headline(n),
        )
        cells = [f"{n:>10}"] + [f"{str(r):>10}" for r in results]
        print("  " + "  ".join(cells))

    print("\nAll properties confirmed for n = 1..5.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Future Directions — Tightness of the Isolation Lemma under edge offsets

This cycle established, for the singleton hypergraph with an arbitrary integer
edge offset, an exact product–sum formula for the number of isolating weight
assignments, and identified its two extreme regimes: constant offsets reproduce
the Faber–Harris extremal value `n · ∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}`, while widely separated
offsets isolate every assignment and reach the maximum `d^n`. The following
conjectures extend these findings.

## Conjecture 1 — Offset monotonicity of the isolating count

For the singleton hypergraph, the isolating count is minimised exactly at the
constant offsets: every integer offset `f` satisfies
`I(n,d,f) ≥ n · ∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}`, with equality iff `f` is constant.

The key insight is that spreading the offsets apart can only *break* ties in
favour of a unique minimiser, never create them, so the symmetric offset sits at
the bottom of the count and any deviation strictly increases the number of
isolating assignments. Why now? The exact product–sum formula reduces the claim
to a term-by-term comparison of "above threshold" cardinalities against their
symmetric baseline, turning a global extremal statement into a local, checkable
inequality.

## Conjecture 2 — Full offset spectrum

As `f` ranges over all integer offsets, the isolating count `I(n,d,f)` takes
*every* integer value in the interval `[ n · ∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}, d^n ]` and no value
outside it.

The key insight is that the constant and separated offsets realise the two
endpoints, and interpolating one coordinate of the offset at a time changes the
count by controlled increments, sweeping out the whole interval. Why now? Both
endpoints are now pinned down exactly, so the remaining task is a connectivity
argument on the offset lattice rather than a search for the extremes.

## Conjecture 3 — General inclusion-free hypergraphs attain the lower bound

For every inclusion-free hypergraph `H` on `n` vertices there exists an edge
offset `f` for which the number of isolating assignments equals the Faber–Harris
lower bound `n · ∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}` exactly.

The key insight is that a carefully chosen offset can force every edge except a
minimal "spanning skeleton" to be non-competitive, reducing the isolating
structure of an arbitrary Sperner family to that of the singleton hypergraph
already solved here. Why now? The singleton case is the offset-free anchor; with
its exact count in hand, the general statement becomes a question of transporting
that count along an offset that collapses `H` onto its skeleton.

+
+Experiment: enumeration gave isolating count `21` for the offset `(0,1,5)` on
+`(n,d)=(3,3)` (strictly above the offset-free `15`), `42` for every constant
+offset on `(3,4)` (equal to the offset-free value), and `d^n` for the separated
+offsets `f i = i·d` (`64` on `(3,4)`).  The per-vertex product formula
+`∑_m ∏_{j≠i} #{k : f i + m < f j + k}` matched brute force on all sampled offsets.
+
+Analysis: fixing the (unique) argmin vertex `i` and its value `m`, the remaining
+`n-1` coordinates range independently over the values exceeding the offset-shifted
+threshold `f i + m - f j`, so the count factors as a product of one-dimensional
+"above threshold" cardinalities.  Constant offsets cancel the shift and restore
+the `(d-1-m)^{n-1}` factors; separated offsets push one threshold below `0`,
+trivialising every factor to the full range.
+
+Critique: the count is genuine — for separated offsets the isolating set is all of
+`[d]^n`, and for constant offsets it agrees set-theoretically with the offset-free
+isolating set (via the `∃!`/strict-min bridge).  The witness
+`offset_changes_count` refutes any claim that the extremal value is an offset
+invariant.
+
+Synthesis: `card_isolatingSetF_eq` is the master identity; `card_isolatingSetF_const`
+reuses `card_isolating_singleton_eq`, and `card_isolatingSetF_separated` pins the
+opposite extreme.
+-/
+
+namespace Offsets
+
+/-- Weight of the singleton edge `{i}` under offset `f` and assignment `w`. -/
+def gWeight (f : Fin n → ℤ) (w : Fin n → Fin d) (i : Fin n) : ℤ := f i + (w i : ℤ)
+
+/-- `w` is **isolating** for offset `f` when a unique vertex attains the minimum
+offset-weight. -/
+def IsIsolatingF (f : Fin n → ℤ) (w : Fin n → Fin d) : Prop :=
+  ∃! i, ∀ j, gWeight f w i ≤ gWeight f w j
+
+/-- Strict formulation: some vertex is a *strict* offset-weight minimum. -/
+def HasStrictMinF (f : Fin n → ℤ) (w : Fin n → Fin d) : Prop :=
+  ∃ i, ∀ j, j ≠ i → gWeight f w i < gWeight f w j
+
+/-- The two notions of "isolating" coincide for every offset. -/
+theorem isIsolatingF_iff_hasStrictMinF (f : Fin n → ℤ) (w : Fin n → Fin d) :
+    IsIsolatingF f w ↔ HasStrictMinF f w := by
+  constructor
+  · rintro ⟨i, hi, huniq⟩
+    refine ⟨i, fun j hj => ?_⟩
+    rcases lt_or_eq_of_le (hi j) with h | h
+    · exact h
+    · exact absurd (huniq j (fun k => h ▸ hi k)) hj
+  · rintro ⟨i, hi⟩
+    refine ⟨i, fun j => ?_, fun k hk => ?_⟩
+    · rcases eq_or_ne j i with rfl | hj
+      · exact le_refl _
+      · exact le_of_lt (hi j hj)
+    · by_contra hne
+      exact absurd (hk i) (not_le.mpr (hi k hne))
+
+/-- The set of isolating assignments for offset `f`. -/
+noncomputable def isolatingSetF (f : Fin n → ℤ) : Finset (Fin n → Fin d) :=
+  Finset.univ.filter (fun w => HasStrictMinF f w)
+
+/-- The set of assignments for which vertex `i` is the strict offset-weight
+minimum. -/
+noncomputable def strictMinAtF (f : Fin n → ℤ) (i : Fin n) : Finset (Fin n → Fin d) :=
+  Finset.univ.filter (fun w => ∀ j, j ≠ i → gWeight f w i < gWeight f w j)
+
+/-
+For a fixed argmin vertex `i` and minimum value `m`, the strict-min fiber
+factors as a product of one-dimensional "above threshold" cardinalities.
+-/
+theorem card_fiberF (f : Fin n → ℤ) (i : Fin n) (m : Fin d) :
+    (Finset.univ.filter
+        (fun w : Fin n → Fin d =>
+          w i = m ∧ ∀ j, j ≠ i → f i + (m : ℤ) < f j + (w j : ℤ))).card
+      = ∏ j ∈ Finset.univ.erase i,
+          (Finset.univ.filter (fun k : Fin d => f i + (m : ℤ) < f j + (k : ℤ))).card := by
+  set t : Fin n → Finset (Fin d) := fun j => if j = i then {m} else Finset.filter (fun k => f i + (m : ℤ) < f j + (k : ℤ)) Finset.univ;
+  convert Fintype.card_piFinset t using 1;
+  · convert rfl;
+    grind;
+  · rw [ ← Finset.prod_erase_mul _ _ ( Finset.mem_univ i ), Finset.prod_congr rfl ] ; aesop;
+    aesop
+
+/-

+minimum value `m` of the product of "above threshold" counts.
+-/
+theorem card_strictMinAtF (f : Fin n → ℤ) (i : Fin n) :
+    (strictMinAtF (d := d) f i).card
+      = ∑ m : Fin d, ∏ j ∈ Finset.univ.erase i,
+          (Finset.univ.filter (fun k : Fin d => f i + (m : ℤ) < f j + (k : ℤ))).card := by
+  rw [ show strictMinAtF f i = Finset.biUnion ( Finset.univ : Finset ( Fin d ) ) ( fun m => Finset.univ.filter ( fun w : Fin n → Fin d => w i = m ∧ ∀ j, j ≠ i → f i + ( m : ℤ ) < f j + ( w j : ℤ ) ) ) from ?_ ];
+  · rw [ Finset.card_biUnion ];
+    · exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun _ _ => card_fiberF f i _;
+    · exact fun x _ y _ hxy => Finset.disjoint_left.mpr fun w hw₁ hw₂ => hxy <| by aesop;
+  · ext w; simp [strictMinAtF];
+    rfl
+
+/-
+The isolating set is the disjoint union of the strict-min-at-`i` sets.
+-/
+theorem isolatingSetF_card_eq_sum (f : Fin n → ℤ) :
+    (isolatingSetF (d := d) f).card = ∑ i : Fin n, (strictMinAtF (d := d) f i).card := by
+  rw [ ← Finset.card_biUnion ];
+  · congr;
+    ext w; simp [isolatingSetF, strictMinAtF, HasStrictMinF];
+  · intros i hi j hj hij; simp_all +decide [ Finset.disjoint_left, strictMinAtF ] ;
+    exact fun w hw => ⟨ i, by tauto, le_of_lt ( hw j ( by tauto ) ) ⟩
+
+/-- **Exact isolating count for an arbitrary edge offset.**  For the singleton
+hypergraph with offset `f`, the number of isolating assignments in `[d]^n` is the
+product–sum over argmin vertex `i`, minimum value `m`, and the remaining vertices
+`j`, of the number of values exceeding the offset-shifted threshold. -/
+theorem card_isolatingSetF_eq (f : Fin n → ℤ) :
+    (isolatingSetF (d := d) f).card
+      = ∑ i : Fin n, ∑ m : Fin d, ∏ j ∈ Finset.univ.erase i,
+          (Finset.univ.filter (fun k : Fin d => f i + (m : ℤ) < f j + (k : ℤ))).card := by
+  rw [isolatingSetF_card_eq_sum]
+  exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun i _ => card_strictMinAtF f i
+
+/-
+A constant offset does not change which vertex is the strict minimum, so it
+reduces to the offset-free notion `HasStrictMin`.
+-/
+theorem hasStrictMinF_const_iff (c : ℤ) (w : Fin n → Fin d) :
+    HasStrictMinF (fun _ => c) w ↔ HasStrictMin w := by
+  simp [HasStrictMinF, HasStrictMin, gWeight]
+
+/-
+**Constant offsets recover the extremal Faber–Harris value.**  For any
+constant offset the isolating count equals `n · ∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}`, the offset-free
+extremal value of `card_isolating_singleton_eq`.
+-/
+theorem card_isolatingSetF_const (c : ℤ) :
+    (isolatingSetF (fun _ => c) : Finset (Fin n → Fin d)).card
+      = n * ∑ j ∈ Finset.range d, j ^ (n - 1) := by
+  convert IsolationTightness.card_isolating_singleton_eq n d using 1;
+  exact congr_arg _ ( Finset.filter_congr fun x _ => hasStrictMinF_const_iff c x )
+
+/-
+**Widely separated offsets isolate every assignment.**  With the geometrically
+separated offset `f i = i · d`, vertex `0` is always the strict minimum, so every
+assignment is isolating and the count attains its maximum `d^n`.
+-/
+theorem card_isolatingSetF_separated (hn : 0 < n) :
+    (isolatingSetF (fun i => (i : ℤ) * d) : Finset (Fin n → Fin d)).card = d ^ n := by
+  -- Show that every assignment is isolating with vertex `0` as the strict minimum.
+  have h_all_isolating : ∀ w : Fin n → Fin d, HasStrictMinF (fun i : Fin n => (i : ℤ) * d) w := by
+    intro w;
+    use ⟨ 0, hn ⟩ ; intro j hj; simp +decide [ *, gWeight ] ;
+    nlinarith [ show ( j : ℕ ) > 0 from Nat.pos_of_ne_zero fun h => hj <| Fin.ext h, Fin.is_lt ( w ⟨ 0, hn ⟩ ), Fin.is_lt ( w j ) ];
+  rw [ show isolatingSetF ( fun i : Fin n => ( i : ℤ ) * d ) = Finset.univ from Finset.filter_true_of_mem fun w _ => h_all_isolating w, Finset.card_univ ] ; norm_num [ Finset.card_univ ]
+
+/-- Computable count of isolating assignments for an integer offset. -/
+def isoCountF (n d : ℕ) (f : Fin n → ℤ) : ℕ :=
+  (Finset.univ.filter
+    (fun w : Fin n → Fin d => ∃ i, ∀ j, j ≠ i → f i + (w i : ℤ) < f j + (w j : ℤ))).card
+
+/-- The computable mirror agrees with the abstract isolating count. -/
+theorem isoCountF_eq_card (f : Fin n → ℤ) :
+    isoCountF n d f = (isolatingSetF (d := d) f).card := by
+  rw [isoCountF, isolatingSetF]
+  congr 1
+  exact Finset.filter_congr_decidable _ (fun w => HasStrictMinF f w) _
+
+/-- A constant offset attains the offset-free extremal value `42 = 3·(0²+1²+2²+3²)`. -/
+example : isoCountF 3 4 (fun _ => 7) = 42 := by decide
+
+/-- Separated offsets isolate everything: the count reaches the maximum `d^n`. -/
+example : isoCountF 2 2 (fun i => (i : ℤ) * 2) = 4 := by decide
+
+/-- **Offsets genuinely change the isolating count.**  The offset `(0,3)` on
+`(n,d)=(2,2)` isolates all four assignments, whereas the offset-free count is only
+two — the extremal Faber–Harris value is not an offset invariant. -/
+theorem offset_changes_count :
+    isoCountF 2 2 (![0, 3]) ≠ isoCountF 2 2 (fun _ => 0) := by decide
+
+end Offsets
+
 end IsolationTightness

# Computational Evidence — Isolation Lemma tightness under arbitrary edge offsets

Setting: the singleton hypergraph on `n` vertices with integer edge offset
`f : Fin n → ℤ`. Edge `{v}` has weight `f v + w v`, and an assignment
`w ∈ [d]^n` is *isolating* when a unique vertex attains the strict minimum of
`v ↦ f v + w v`. We write `I(n,d,f)` for the number of isolating assignments.

## 1. Small-case calculations

Direct enumeration (all `d^n` assignments) gives:

| n | d | offset f            | I(n,d,f) | offset-free `n·∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}` |
|---|---|---------------------|----------|---------------------------------|
| 3 | 4 | (0,0,0)             | 42       | 42                              |
| 3 | 4 | (7,7,7)             | 42       | 42                              |
| 3 | 3 | (0,0,0)             | 15       | 15                              |
| 3 | 3 | (0,1,5)             | 21       | 15                              |
| 2 | 2 | (0,0)               | 2        | 2                               |
| 2 | 2 | (0,3)               | 4        | 2                               |
| 3 | 4 | (0,4,8)  [= i·d]    | 64       | 42                              |
| 2 | 2 | (0,2)    [= i·d]    | 4        | 2                               |

Observations:
* **Constant offsets** reproduce the offset-free extremal value exactly.
* **Generic offsets** (e.g. `(0,1,5)`) strictly exceed it.
* **Separated offsets** `f i = i·d` isolate *every* assignment: `I = d^n`.

## 2. Per-vertex product formula

For every sampled offset the identity

`I(n,d,f) = ∑_i ∑_{m<d} ∏_{j≠i} #{k<d : f i + m < f j + k}`

matched brute force on `(n,d,f)` in
`{(3,4,(0,1,5)), (2,3,(2,0)), (3,3,(0,0,0)), (4,3,(0,1,2,1))}` — all `true`.

## 3. Counterexample hunt (is the extremal value offset-invariant?)

Refuted immediately: `I(2,2,(0,3)) = 4 ≠ 2 = I(2,2,(0,0))`. Hence the
Faber–Harris extremal value `n·∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}` is **not** an offset invariant; it
is the value of the symmetric (constant-offset) regime.

## 4. Sequence note

The offset-free diagonal `n·∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}` for `n=3` is `0,0,3,15,42,90,…`
(the value `3·∑_{j<d} j^2`). Constant offsets leave this fixed; separated offsets
send it to the maximal `d^n`.

All computations above are reproduced by the `#eval`/`decide` checks embedded in
`IsolationLemmaTightness.lean`.

# Future Directions — Tightness of the Isolation Lemma under edge offsets

This cycle established, for the singleton hypergraph with an arbitrary integer
edge offset, an exact product–sum formula for the number of isolating weight
assignments, and identified its two extreme regimes: constant offsets reproduce
the Faber–Harris extremal value `n · ∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}`, while widely separated
offsets isolate every assignment and reach the maximum `d^n`. The following
conjectures extend these findings.

## Conjecture 1 — Offset monotonicity of the isolating count

For the singleton hypergraph, the isolating count is minimised exactly at the
constant offsets: every integer offset `f` satisfies
`I(n,d,f) ≥ n · ∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}`, with equality iff `f` is constant.

The key insight is that spreading the offsets apart can only *break* ties in
favour of a unique minimiser, never create them, so the symmetric offset sits at
the bottom of the count and any deviation strictly increases the number of
isolating assignments. Why now? The exact product–sum formula reduces the claim
to a term-by-term comparison of "above threshold" cardinalities against their
symmetric baseline, turning a global extremal statement into a local, checkable
inequality.

## Conjecture 2 — Full offset spectrum

As `f` ranges over all integer offsets, the isolating count `I(n,d,f)` takes
*every* integer value in the interval `[ n · ∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}, d^n ]` and no value
outside it.

The key insight is that the constant and separated offsets realise the two
endpoints, and interpolating one coordinate of the offset at a time changes the
count by controlled increments, sweeping out the whole interval. Why now? Both
endpoints are now pinned down exactly, so the remaining task is a connectivity
argument on the offset lattice rather than a search for the extremes.

## Conjecture 3 — General inclusion-free hypergraphs attain the lower bound

For every inclusion-free hypergraph `H` on `n` vertices there exists an edge
offset `f` for which the number of isolating assignments equals the Faber–Harris
lower bound `n · ∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}` exactly.

The key insight is that a carefully chosen offset can force every edge except a
minimal "spanning skeleton" to be non-competitive, reducing the isolating
structure of an arbitrary Sperner family to that of the singleton hypergraph
already solved here. Why now? The singleton case is the offset-free anchor; with
its exact count in hand, the general statement becomes a question of transporting
that count along an offset that collapses `H` onto its skeleton.

## Conjecture 4 — Real versus integer offsets

The set of isolating-count values achievable with real offsets coincides with
the set achievable with integer offsets; passing to the reals adds no new counts.

The key insight is that the isolating condition depends only on the linear order
of the finitely many edge weights, and any real offset can be perturbed to a
rational — then cleared to an integer — without crossing a tie. Why now? The
integer theory is now exact, so the reduction from real to integer offsets is the
only missing link to the full real-valued Isolation Lemma statement.

## Conjecture 5 — Offset that maximises uniqueness margin

Among all offsets achieving the maximal count `d^n`, the separated offset
`f i = i·d` minimises the total number of distinct edge-weight values used, and
is optimal for the "isolation margin" (the smallest gap between the minimum edge
weight and the runner-up) in a precise `1/`-scaling sense.

The key insight is that geometric separation by exactly the vertex range `d` is
the tightest spacing that still guarantees a global order of edges independent of
the assignment. Why now? The separated construction is already shown to saturate
the count; quantifying *how efficiently* it does so is the natural next question
and connects the counting bound to the quantitative margin that the Isolation
Lemma is usually applied through.

# Future Directions — The Topology of Argumentation (V): Stable Extensions

This cycle deepens the formalization of Dung's abstract argumentation theory and
the conflict-free complex `K(AF)` by adding the **stable extension** — the
strongest of the classical extension-based semantics — and placing it inside the
full semantic hierarchy and the Euler/semantics bridge.

New self-contained file: `Catalog/Novelty/ArgumentationStable.lean`.

## What is proved

A set `S` of arguments is a **stable extension** when it is conflict-free and it
*attacks every argument it does not contain*:
`Stable R S := ConflictFree R S ∧ ∀ a ∉ S, ∃ b ∈ S, R b a`.
These are the "no abstention" positions: every argument is accepted or defeated.

### The stable hierarchy (general frameworks)

Each result feeds the next, forming a chain
`stable ⟹ preferred ⟹ complete ⟹ admissible ⟹ conflict-free`:

* `stable_defends` — a stable set defends each of its members.
* `stable_admissible` — every stable extension is admissible.
* `stable_complete` — every stable extension is complete (closed under defense).
* `stable_preferred` — every stable extension is preferred (maximal admissible).
* `stable_maximalConflictFree` — every stable extension is a *facet* of `K(AF)`.
* `groundedExt_subset_stable` — the grounded (skeptical) extension lies inside
  every stable extension.

### The symmetric collapse

For **symmetric irreflexive** frameworks (mutual disagreement without
self-attack) the top of the hierarchy collapses:

* `maximalConflictFree_stable_of_symmetric` — every facet is stable.
* `stable_iff_preferred_of_symmetric_irrefl` —
  **stable ⇔ preferred ⇔ facet of `K(AF)`**.

### The stable Euler bridge

For the complete conflict graph `completeAF n` (symmetric and irreflexive):

* `stable_completeAF_iff` — the stable extensions are exactly the singletons.
* `stable_completeAF_ncard` — there are exactly `n` of them.
* `euler_completeAF` — the Euler characteristic of `K(AF)` is `n`.
* `euler_eq_stable_completeAF` — **`χ(K(AF)) = #{stable extensions}`** for `n ≥ 1`.

This extends the Euler/semantics bridge of `ArgumentationSymmetric` (previously
stated for preferred extensions) to stable extensions.

All results compile under Lean 4 / Mathlib (`v4.28.0`) with no `sorry` and depend
only on the standard axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`.

## Open directions

* **General symmetric frameworks.** Extend `stable_iff_preferred_of_symmetric_irrefl`
  and the Euler bridge from the complete conflict graph to arbitrary symmetric
  irreflexive frameworks, expressing `χ(K(AF))` via the independence complex of
  the conflict graph.
* **Existence gap.** Unlike preferred extensions, stable extensions need not
  exist. Characterize the frameworks that admit at least one stable extension
  (e.g. formalize that finite frameworks whose conflict graph is symmetric always
  do, via maximal independent sets).
* **Full homology.** Replace the Euler characteristic by the reduced homology of
  `K(AF)` and relate its Betti numbers to the fine structure of the semantics.

import Mathlib

/-!
# The topology of argumentation, VI: the existence gap for stable extensions

This file is **self-contained** (it re-declares the basic Dung semantics) and
pursues, in *contrarian* mode, the **existence gap** left open by
`ArgumentationStable.lean`:

> Unlike preferred extensions, **stable extensions need not exist.**

We formulate four bold conjectures about the existence of stable extensions and
settle each one, proving two and disproving two.

## Bold conjectures, settled

* **`no_stable_cycle3`** — *Disproves* "every finite framework has a stable
  extension": the odd 3-cycle `0 → 1 → 2 → 0` has **no** stable extension.
* **`cycle3_preferred_not_stable`** — *Disproves* "every preferred extension is
  stable": in the 3-cycle the empty set is a preferred (indeed the unique
  admissible) extension, yet it is not stable.  So the strict inclusion
  `stable ⊊ preferred` of `ArgumentationStable.lean` is genuinely strict.
* **`stable_exists_of_finite_symmetric_irrefl`** — *Proves* "every finite
  symmetric irreflexive framework has a stable extension" (the existence gap
  closes on the symmetric side): a maximal conflict-free set exists by finiteness
  and is stable.
* **`no_stable_of_reflexive`** / **`no_stable_reflAF`** — *Disproves* "symmetry
  alone suffices for existence": a symmetric framework with a self-attack (hence
  reflexive) and at least one argument has no stable extension.  Irreflexivity in
  the previous item is therefore necessary.

Quantitatively, `stable_cycle3_ncard` records that the number of stable
extensions of the 3-cycle is `0`, in contrast with the count `n` for the
complete conflict graph (`ArgumentationStable.stable_completeAF_ncard`).
-/

namespace ArgStableGap

open Finset

variable {A : Type*} (R : A → A → Prop)

/-! ## Basic Dung semantics (self-contained) -/

/-- `S` is *conflict-free*: no argument in `S` attacks another in `S`. -/
def ConflictFree (S : Set A) : Prop := ∀ a ∈ S, ∀ b ∈ S, ¬ R a b

/-- `S` *defends* `a`: every attacker of `a` is counter-attacked from `S`. -/
def Defends (S : Set A) (a : A) : Prop := ∀ b, R b a → ∃ c ∈ S, R c b

/-- `S` is *admissible*: conflict-free and defends all its members. -/
def Admissible (S : Set A) : Prop := ConflictFree R S ∧ ∀ a ∈ S, Defends R S a

/-- `S` is a **preferred extension**: a maximal admissible set. -/
def Preferred (S : Set A) : Prop :=
  Admissible R S ∧ ∀ T, Admissible R T → S ⊆ T → T = S

/-- `S` is **maximal conflict-free**: a facet of the conflict-free complex. -/
def MaximalConflictFree (S : Set A) : Prop :=
  ConflictFree R S ∧ ∀ T, ConflictFree R T → S ⊆ T → T = S

/-- `S` is a **stable extension**: conflict-free and it attacks every argument it
does not contain. -/
def Stable (S : Set A) : Prop :=
  ConflictFree R S ∧ ∀ a, a ∉ S → ∃ b ∈ S, R b a

/-! ## The symmetric collapse (re-proved, self-contained) -/

/-- In a symmetric framework every conflict-free set is admissible. -/
theorem conflictFree_admissible_of_symmetric (hsym : Symmetric R) {S : Set A}
    (hS : ConflictFree R S) : Admissible R S :=
  ⟨hS, fun a ha _ hb => ⟨a, ha, hsym hb⟩⟩

/-- In a symmetric irreflexive framework every maximal conflict-free set is
stable. -/

# Computational Evidence — Stable Extensions: the Existence Gap

This cycle (contrarian mode) targets **existence and non-existence of stable
extensions**, the open direction flagged in the previous cycle
(`ArgumentationStable.lean`): *unlike preferred extensions, stable extensions
need not exist.*

## Bold conjectures under test

1. **(C1, existence)** Every finite argumentation framework has a stable
   extension. — **DISPROVED** (odd cycle).
2. **(C2)** Every preferred extension is stable. — **DISPROVED** (odd cycle).
3. **(C3, positive)** Every finite *symmetric irreflexive* framework has a
   stable extension. — **PROVED**.
4. **(C4)** Irreflexivity is unnecessary in C3: every finite symmetric framework
   has a stable extension. — **DISPROVED** (self-attacks).

## Small-case enumeration (brute force over all subsets)

Framework `cycle3` on `Fin 3`: `R a b ↔ b = a + 1`, i.e. `0→1→2→0`.

| framework            | #conflict-free | #admissible | #preferred | #stable |
|----------------------|:--------------:|:-----------:|:----------:|:-------:|
| `cycle3` (3-cycle)   |       7        |      1      |     1      |  **0**  |
| complete graph `K_3` |       4        |      4      |     3      |    3    |

Computed by filtering `Finset (Finset (Fin 3))`:

- `#{S | ConflictFree cycle3 S ∧ dominates}` = **0**  → no stable extension.
- `#{S | Admissible cycle3 S}` = **1**, that single set has cardinality `0`
  (the empty set). Hence `∅` is the unique admissible = grounded = **preferred**
  extension, and it is *not* stable. This witnesses both C1 and C2 being false.
- For the complete graph `K_3` (symmetric, irreflexive) the stable count is `3`,
  matching the `n` singletons — consistent with `ArgumentationStable.lean`.

## Why the 3-cycle has no stable extension (hand proof)

`Stable S` needs `S` conflict-free and: `a ∉ S ⇒ (a-1) ∈ S` (the unique attacker
of `a` is `a-1`).

- If `0 ∈ S`: then `1 ∉ S` (else `0` attacks `1`, a conflict). Also `2 ∉ S`
  (else `2` attacks `0`). But `2 ∉ S` forces its attacker `1 ∈ S`,
  contradicting `1 ∉ S`.
- If `0 ∉ S`: its attacker `2 ∈ S`. Then `1 ∉ S` (else `1` attacks `2`). But
  `1 ∉ S` forces its attacker `0 ∈ S`, contradiction.

So no `S` is stable. The same argument works for every odd cycle.

## Why symmetric + reflexive can fail (C4)

If `R a a` for some/all `a`, no nonempty set is conflict-free, so the only
conflict-free set is `∅`; but `∅` is stable only if it attacks every argument,
impossible when the framework is nonempty. Concretely `reflAF : Fin 1` with
`R _ _ = True` is symmetric and has **no** stable extension.

## Why symmetric + irreflexive always succeeds (C3)

On a finite type the conflict-free sets form a nonempty finite family, hence a
maximal one `S` exists. In a symmetric irreflexive framework a maximal
conflict-free set is stable (proved in `ArgumentationStable.lean` as
`maximalConflictFree_stable_of_symmetric`): any `a ∉ S` must conflict with some
`b ∈ S`, and symmetry turns that conflict into an attack `R b a`.

All four findings are formalized in `Catalog/Novelty/ArgumentationStableGap.lean`.

# Future Directions — The Topology of Argumentation (VI): the existence gap for stable extensions

This cycle (contrarian mode) attacks the **existence gap** left open by the
previous cycle's `Catalog/Novelty/ArgumentationStable.lean`:

> Unlike preferred extensions, **stable extensions need not exist.**

New self-contained file: `Catalog/Novelty/ArgumentationStableGap.lean`
(Lean 4 / Mathlib `v4.28.0`, no `sorry`, axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`,
`Quot.sound`).

## Bold conjectures, settled

We formulated four bold conjectures on the existence of stable extensions and
settled each — proving two and disproving two.

| # | Conjecture | Verdict | Theorem |
|---|------------|---------|---------|
| C1 | Every finite framework has a stable extension | **DISPROVED** | `no_stable_cycle3` |
| C2 | Every preferred extension is stable | **DISPROVED** | `cycle3_preferred_not_stable` |
| C3 | Every finite symmetric irreflexive framework has a stable extension | **PROVED** | `stable_exists_of_finite_symmetric_irrefl` |
| C4 | Symmetry alone suffices for existence (C3 without irreflexivity) | **DISPROVED** | `no_stable_reflAF` |

### C1 / C2 — the odd cycle refutations

The directed 3-cycle `cycle3 : 0 → 1 → 2 → 0` (`R a b ↔ b = a + 1` on `Fin 3`) is
irreflexive (`cycle3_irreflexive`) and *not* symmetric (`cycle3_not_symmetric`).

* `no_stable_cycle3` — the 3-cycle has **no** stable extension, refuting C1.
* `stable_cycle3_ncard` — quantitatively, `#{stable extensions} = 0` (contrast
  the count `n` for the complete conflict graph in `ArgumentationStable.lean`).
* `cycle3_admissible_empty`, `cycle3_preferred_empty` — the empty set is the
  unique admissible set, hence a preferred extension of the 3-cycle.
* `cycle3_empty_not_stable`, `cycle3_preferred_not_stable` — but `∅` is not
  stable, so `stable ⊊ preferred` is a **strict** inclusion (refuting C2 and
  sharpening `ArgumentationStable.stable_preferred`).

### C3 — existence on the symmetric side

* `exists_maximalConflictFree` — on a finite type a maximal conflict-free set
  (a facet of `K(AF)`) always exists.
* `maximalConflictFree_stable_of_symmetric` — in a symmetric irreflexive
  framework every facet is stable (re-proved self-contained).
* `stable_exists_of_finite_symmetric_irrefl` — hence **every finite symmetric
  irreflexive framework admits a stable extension**, closing the existence gap
  on the symmetric side.

### C4 — irreflexivity is necessary

* `no_stable_of_reflexive` — any nonempty framework in which every argument
  attacks itself has no stable extension (only `∅` is conflict-free, and `∅`
  cannot dominate a nonempty universe).
* `no_stable_reflAF` — the concrete symmetric one-argument self-attack framework
  `reflAF` therefore has no stable extension: symmetry alone does not save C3;
  irreflexivity is genuinely needed.

## Computational evidence

`ComputationalEvidence.md` records the brute-force enumeration over all subsets
of `Fin 3` that motivated these results: the 3-cycle has `1` admissible (the
empty set), `1` preferred, and `0` stable extensions, while the complete graph
`K_3` has `3` stable extensions.

## Open directions

* **Characterize existence in general.** Give a purely combinatorial criterion
  (beyond symmetry) on `(A, R)` guaranteeing a stable extension; e.g. relate it
  to the absence of odd directed cycles among self-defended arguments, or to the
  independence complex of the underlying conflict graph having a full-dimensional
  facet.
* **Counting the gap.** For random or structured frameworks, study
  `#{preferred} − #{stable}` as a numeric invariant of the "abstention" forced
  by odd cycles.
* **Topology of non-existence.** Interpret the vanishing of stable extensions
  (`stable_cycle3_ncard = 0`) homologically: relate it to the reduced homology
  of `K(AF)` for directed (non-symmetric) frameworks, extending the Euler bridge
  of `ArgumentationSymmetric`/`ArgumentationStable` beyond the symmetric case.
